title: 9 best video hook patterns and the research behind them
summary: Learn nine video hook patterns, what the research says about the first seconds of an ad and how to test and produce enough hooks to find the ones that perform.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


Most video hooks fail because they introduce instead of interrupt, and TikTok reports that 90% of ad recall impact is captured in the first six seconds. This guide breaks hooks into nine patterns, from the problem strike to the credible face, and shows what the research says about faces, logos and where viewers actually look. It also covers how to test openings properly and why finding the hooks that perform means producing a lot of them.


Every video ad has two jobs. First, get people to watch. Second, persuade them. **If the first few seconds don't grab attention, the persuasion part might as well not exist.**


TikTok's[creative best practices](https://ads.tiktok.com/business/en/blog/creative-best-practices-top-performing-ads) note that 90% of ad recall impact is captured within the first six seconds. Amazon's[Sponsored Products video guide](https://advertising.amazon.com/library/guides/sponsored-products-video) shares that CTR jumps 8x for the 20% of shoppers who watch past the first five seconds. Those viewers are also 2x more likely to buy from the brand within seven days.


Why do viewers decide so fast?[Taryn Selvan](https://www.linkedin.com/in/taryn-selvan-b68058269) , a post-production specialist at Superside, edits paid social campaigns and multilingual UGC ad sets with multiple hooks per concept, built to test and scale. She says it comes down to recognition:


We're all looking for ourselves. We stay for the things that feel familiar, that make us feel seen or understood.


Taryn Selvan


Post-production Specialist, Superside


Your video hooks are critical to your marketing strategy's success. However, different formats play by different rules.


This article is about video hooks specifically, meaning the opening seconds of video assets. I unpack what the research says, why many video hooks fail and how to test your hooks so your videos deliver results.


Our guide to[social media hooks](https://www.superside.com/blog/social-media-hooks) covers written and post-level hooks across social media platforms. It's a related but different craft.


## The 9 video hook patterns


The nine patterns below offer tried-and-tested ways to get your videos noticed. **Patterns transfer to the next brief. A flat list of examples doesn't.**


Pattern What it does Best for


The problem strike Names the pain point in the first breath Solution-led products


The pattern interrupt Breaks the visual expectation of the feed Crowded categories


The contradiction Makes a bold statement that sounds wrong Category challengers


The demonstration cold open Starts mid-action, with no setup Physical and visual products


The direct address Names the viewer's situation Narrow, definable audiences


The result-first reveal Shows the outcome before the process Transformation stories


The question with stakes Asks something with a real cost attached Considered purchases


The credible face Opens on a person speaking to the camera Trust-led and B2B


The tension build Creates a small unresolved gap Story-led and longer formats


### 1. The problem strike


This hook opens by naming the viewer's pain point first. No brand mention, no setup, no context. Example: "Your best creative is dying in the first two seconds."


**It works because viewers who feel that exact pain self-select instantly.** When the problem is generic, a problem strike turns into just another slogan, and that rarely works.


### 2. The pattern interrupt


This hook shows viewers something they don't expect to see in their feed. Think unusual framing, sudden movement or a visual that doesn't immediately look like an ad.


But beware of interruption without relevance. A pattern interrupt buys you attention, and then you need to keep it. Otherwise, the viewer will scroll past one second later.


**The secret is making the interrupt and the message the same idea.**


Editing does a lot of this work, and sound matters as much as visuals. Taryn builds every opening around music first:


I always start with music. This is the foundation of feeling. Think about any movie. The soundtrack either makes or breaks a powerful moment.


Taryn Selvan


Post-production Specialist, Superside


Then she layers in sound effects:


With sound effects, the video becomes tangible and alive. Go watch any brand ad that you like, pay attention to the sounds, and you'll notice how it draws you in.


Taryn Selvan


Post-production Specialist, Superside


Think of the ticking in a Rolex ad, sneakers hitting gravel in a Nike ad or the hum of a Nespresso machine. Each sound pulls the viewer into the moment.


### 3. The contradiction


This hook opens with something that sounds wrong, then explains why it's true. Example: "Most video hooks waste budget."


It creates a curiosity gap and gives people a reason to keep watching. To keep it from backfiring, make sure you can back up the claim. **If the explanation doesn't live up to the opening, viewers will feel misled.**


### 4. The demonstration cold open


This hook shows your product in action. For a physical product, that might be a stain remover lifting a mark from a shirt. For B2B software, it could be a screen recording of someone completing a task.


**It gives viewers something useful to watch right away.** They can see what the product does without sitting through an introduction.


### 5. The direct address


This one speaks directly to the people you want to reach by naming their situation in the first line. Example: "If you're running paid social with one creative per campaign..."


**The more specific you are, the easier it is for the right viewers to recognize themselves.** It won't appeal to everyone, and that's fine. You want to attract potential customers.


### 6. The result-first reveal


Start with the outcome, whether it's the finished room, the completed transformation or the savings. Then explain the how.


This flips the natural instinct to build up to a reveal. **It works because it starts with what the viewer really wants: the outcome.**


### 7. The question with stakes


This isn't a rhetorical question, which viewers ignore. It's a question with a real cost attached. Example: "How much of your video budget is being spent on frames nobody sees?"


The distinction matters. **A question that implies the viewer may lose something specific is a strong hook.**


### 8. The credible face


Who delivers a message matters as much as the message itself. Behavioral science calls this "the messenger effect," and research supports this pattern more strongly than any other on this list.


Some of the best hooks open with someone speaking directly to the camera. **The key is credibility, not fame.** A real person who knows the subject well can be more convincing than a polished presenter.


### 9. The tension build


Create a small unresolved gap in the opening seconds to pull the viewer in. This is the only pattern that needs a few seconds to work, so it suits longer formats and story-led work rather than six-second placements.


**Executed badly, it becomes a slow start.**


### How to choose your hook pattern


Don't pick by taste. Choose your pattern based on who you're trying to reach and what they need to see first.


- **People who don't know your brand:** Try a pattern interrupt to catch their eye, a problem strike to name a pain point or a demonstration cold open to show your product in action.
- **B2B buyers who need time to weigh their options:** Address their situation directly, put a credible expert on camera or ask a question that highlights the cost of a problem.
- **People who have already shown interest:** Lead with the result. They already know the problem, so show them what your solution can achieve.
- **Buyers you want to win over from established brands:** Try a contradiction that challenges a familiar belief and gives them a reason to consider your alternative.


## What the research on video hooks says


Research offers useful clues about what to show in a video's opening seconds, when to introduce your brand and where to place the most important detail. **Most of it is older than the industry admits, so the dates matter.**


Finding Source Date Basis


90% of ad recall impact is captured within the first six seconds TikTok 2020 study TikTok internal research


Prioritize the hook within six seconds and introduce the content proposition within three TikTok Current guidance Platform guidance for performance ads


A recognizable face in the first five seconds is linked to higher viewership and brand lift Google and the YouTube Insights Team June 2015 Thousands of TrueView ads across 16 countries, 11 verticals and 170 creative attributes


A message-led opening delivered higher ad recall lift than a watermark-logo opening Think with Google, Unskippable Labs March 2017 Controlled three-variant test


A 30-second cut had a 30% higher view-through rate, but only the 15-second cut drove significant recall lift Think with Google, Is Longer Stronger March 2016 The same ad tested at three lengths


Most viewing attention goes to the center of the screen, and glances at the skip button are brief Lumen Research November 2018 Eye-tracking analysis of 1,000+ YouTube ads


8x higher CTR among the 20% of shoppers who watched Sponsored Products videos for more than five seconds Amazon Ads 2026 Amazon internal US measurement


### The first five seconds and why it still matters


Research from Google and the YouTube Insights Team is 11 years old, but its method is why it still holds up. Their[June 2015 "The First 5 Seconds" report](https://www.thinkwithgoogle.com/_qs/documents/953/creating-youtube-ads-that-break-through-in-a-skippable-world.pdf) analyzed thousands of TrueView ads across 16 countries and 11 verticals, using 170 creative attributes.


Two findings are particularly useful:


1. A recognizable face shown in the first five seconds tends to increase viewership and brand lift.
2. When a brand appears early through a logo or spoken mention, there's an inverse relationship between recall and engagement.


**That second finding is the one most brands still overlook.**


### The branding trade-off tested


[The "Unskippable Labs" report](https://www.thinkwithgoogle.com/_qs/documents/1640/unskippable-labs-how-much-branding-on-youtube-is-too-much.pdf) , published by Think with Google in March 2017, ran a controlled three-variant test isolating what goes into the first five seconds.


View-through rates came in at:


- 30% for medium branding, which featured a watermark logo and traditional voice-over
- 29% for the innovative message, which focused on the experience viewers were about to have rather than the brand
- 27% for the original


Ad recall lift ran +40%, +75% and +71%, respectively.


**The takeaway:** In this test, viewers were more likely to remember the ad when it opened with a message about the experience than with a watermark logo. Showing your logo early isn't always the best way to make your ad memorable.


### Hook length is different from ad length


The["Is Longer Stronger" report](https://www.thinkwithgoogle.com/_qs/documents/341/unskippable-video-advertising-ad-recall-brand-favorability.pdf) , published by Think with Google in March 2016, tested the same ad at three different lengths.


The 30-second version had a 30% higher view-through rate than the 15-second version. But only the 15-second version drove a significant lift in ad recall.


**The takeaway:** Ad length and hook speed are two different decisions. A longer ad can still work, but the best hooks land quickly.


### Where attention actually goes


[Lumen Research's eye-tracking analysis](https://lumen-research.com/blog/secrets-of-the-skip-button/) of more than 1,000 YouTube ads found that viewers glance at the skip button only briefly and spend most of their viewing time looking at the center of the screen.


For your video hooks, this suggests a simple starting point. **Put the product, person or action you want viewers to notice near the center of the frame.** Don't leave a key detail small or tucked into a corner.


### Be careful of bold claims about video hooks


There's no credible, published benchmark for video hook rate or thumbstop rate. Many articles quote figures for these metrics, but they trace back to claims I couldn't verify. **A widely repeated idea is that people give an ad just 2.5 seconds of attention. I couldn't find evidence to back it up** , so I've left it out.


## Why so many video hooks fail


A weak video hook usually takes too long to get to the point or gives viewers too little reason to keep watching. Here are five common problems to watch for.


### Failure 1: It starts with an introduction


**What it looks like:** "Hi, we're X, and today we're going to..."


**The fix:** Start with the problem, action or result. Cut the greeting and tell viewers something useful straight away.


Taryn sees this mistake more than any other:


Burying the hook. So many openings spend the first essential seconds on a name, a greeting or what the video is 'going to be about' (yawn). That just won't land with a stranger mid-scroll because it doesn't feel worth their time. Lead with the juicy bits!


Taryn Selvan


Post-production Specialist, Superside


### Failure 2: It's too generic


**What it looks like:** "Want to grow your business?" could apply to almost anyone, so it gives your audience little reason to pay attention.


**The fix:** Name a situation or pain point your potential customers will recognize. "Running paid social with one creative per campaign?" gives them a much clearer reason to listen.


### Failure 3: The main subject is hard to see


**What it looks like:** The product or action is small, off to one side or lost in a busy frame.


**The fix:** Make the main subject easy to spot. Placing it near the center of the frame is a useful starting point.


### Failure 4: It opens with a logo and nothing else


**What it looks like:** A logo animation delays the message or demonstration.


**The fix:** Give viewers a reason to watch from the first frame. You can still show your brand early through the product, packaging or other recognizable brand elements.


### Failure 5: It promises more than the video delivers


**What it looks like:** A bold claim or dramatic reveal leads to an explanation that doesn't live up to it.


**The fix:** Make sure the rest of the video delivers what the opening promises. If it doesn't, adjust the hook or strengthen the content that follows.


**Tip:** Watch the video without its first three seconds. If the message still makes sense, you may have found a stronger opening.


When it comes to picking the opening shot, Taryn's rule is simple:


I choose the one I'm most proud of. If I'm not excited by the first shot, why would the viewer be? The first shot hints at what's coming, so it has to be the best one to give the viewer a reason to stay.


Taryn Selvan


Post-production Specialist, Superside


## How to test your video hooks


Testing different openings helps you understand what makes your audience keep watching and take action. **Keep comparisons clean and measure against your campaign goals.**


Before you spend budget, gut-check the opening yourself. Taryn's test:


I try to watch it as if I am the viewer scrolling past this video for the very first time. And then if I feel a sense of curiosity or a sort of lift in energy, it's working.


Taryn Selvan


Post-production Specialist, Superside


- **Change the video hook and keep the rest consistent:** Use the same video body, music and end card across variants. Keep targeting and delivery conditions comparable, too. This makes it easier to see whether the opening drove the difference.
- **Match the number of variants to your budget:** Two openings can give you a useful comparison. Testing more lets you explore different approaches, but each one needs enough delivery to judge its performance. Don't spread a small budget across so many variants that the results become hard to read.
- **Measure against the campaign's goal:** Short viewing metrics show whether an opening holds attention, but read them alongside the results you want. For a conversion campaign, more three-second views alone won't prove one hook performs better.
- **Refresh based on performance:** Monitor results over time and test new openings when performance drops. A weaker result doesn't automatically mean the hook has worn out. Audience saturation, targeting and the offer can also play a role. Our guides to[ad fatigue](https://www.superside.com/blog/ad-fatigue) and[digital ad lifespan](https://www.superside.com/blog/digital-ad-lifespan) explain what to watch for.


For more detail, explore our guides to[creative testing for paid social](https://www.superside.com/blog/creative-testing-framework-paid-social) ,[social creative performance strategies](https://www.superside.com/blog/social-creative-performance-strategies) ,[designing high-performing ads](https://www.superside.com/blog/design-high-performing-ads) and[creative performance](https://www.superside.com/blog/what-is-creative-performance) .


## How to write a video hook: A practical method


When you're staring at a blank brief, work backward to get to a strong hook.


- **Start at the end of the video:** What's the main message you want your audience to take away? Use it to shape an opening that gives them a reason to keep watching.
- **Write ten and keep two:** Writing lots of hooks isn't a sign you're struggling. It's part of the process.
- **Say it out loud:** Hooks are spoken or read in about two seconds. If it needs a breath in the middle, it's too long.
- **Cut the first line:** Then check whether the second line was actually the hook all along.
- **Test it against the pattern list:** If your hook doesn't clearly belong to one of the nine patterns above, it might not be doing anything specific enough to name.


## The production challenge: Creating enough video hooks to test


Everyone can generate. Not everything can perform. **Finding the hooks that perform takes repeated production and testing.** Each concept needs opening variations to compare, plus fresh options as performance changes.


Plan for that volume from the start. Build a library of hooks you can pair with the same core video, then use the results to guide what you produce next.


Teams that win this game take a modular approach: one body, many openings, produced as variants rather than separate videos. **The challenge shifts from making more videos to producing and managing more versions.**


That's why a solid production process matters, from[automated ad creative versioning](https://www.superside.com/blog/automate-ad-creative-versioning) to[scaling short-form video with AI](https://www.superside.com/blog/scaling-short-form-video-ai) . The same shift is shaping current[trends in short-form video](https://www.superside.com/blog/short-form-video-trends) and[AI video](https://www.superside.com/blog/ai-video-trends) .


Polish isn't always an advantage, either. In our own work on[UGC-style ads](https://www.superside.com/blog/smash-your-cpl-with-ugc-style-ads) , less polished creative delivered a 217% increase in lead acquisition and cut our cost per lead by 45% month over month. ## Build better video hooks through testing


Start by checking your video hooks for the five common pitfalls. Then give viewers a good reason to watch. Show the product, person or action clearly, weave your brand into the opening, talk pain points and make sure the rest of the video delivers on the hook.


Finally, test your hooks against your campaign goals and use the results to shape new variations. **That's what separates teams that know which hooks work from teams that just have opinions about it.**

## FAQs


A video hook is the opening of a video, designed to grab attention in the first few seconds and give people a reason to keep watching. It's distinct from the ad's message or offer.


TikTok recommends prioritizing the hook in the first six seconds and introducing the content proposition in the first three. The platform reports that[90% of ad recall impact](https://ads.tiktok.com/business/en/blog/creative-best-practices-top-performing-ads) is captured in that opening window.


Shorter than most teams build. The main platforms suggest landing your hook within the first three to six seconds. Amazon's data shows[CTR jumps 8x](https://advertising.amazon.com/library/guides/sponsored-products-video) among shoppers who watch past the first five seconds.


Specificity and immediacy. The strongest hooks name a problem, situation or outcome in the first moment rather than introducing the brand or setting the scene.


Research from Google's YouTube Insights Team found that[a recognizable face in the first five seconds](https://www.thinkwithgoogle.com/_qs/documents/953/creating-youtube-ads-that-break-through-in-a-skippable-world.pdf) tends to lift viewership and brand lift.[Lumen's eye-tracking work](https://lumen-research.com/blog/secrets-of-the-skip-button/) shows attention is concentrated in the center of the screen.


Be careful.[Google's First 5 Seconds research](https://www.thinkwithgoogle.com/_qs/documents/953/creating-youtube-ads-that-break-through-in-a-skippable-world.pdf) found an inverse relationship between ad recall and engagement when brands appear early through a logo or spoken mention.


[Think with Google's Unskippable Labs test](https://www.thinkwithgoogle.com/_qs/documents/1640/unskippable-labs-how-much-branding-on-youtube-is-too-much.pdf) found an opening message beat an opening logo on recall lift. Branding still matters, but front-loading the logo isn't the way to do it.


At least two, and more if your budget can give each variant enough delivery to read the results. Hold everything after the opening constant so the hook is the only variable. Plan to replace hooks regularly as performance changes.


There's no credible published benchmark, and I'd rather say so than repeat one. Figures for hook rate and thumbstop rate trace back to unsourced content, and the widely quoted claim that viewers give an ad 2.5 seconds of attention couldn't be verified. Benchmark against your own past performance instead.
